## Skills, names and knowledge

**Skills are hard-coded; decisions belong to the character** (decided 18 October 2026). The split applies to every character: envoys, spies, commanders, candidates and outlaws.

- **The engine supplies skill.** A commander's moves come from a tactical search sized by his competence, since a small model is no tactician. What an envoy notices, whether a forgery succeeds and whether a spy is caught stay engine rolls on competence, as today.
- **The character decides what it does.** A model character makes its own choices, informed by its character: its traits written into its persona as values, temptations and fears, its memories, and the rumours it has heard. A greedy envoy should feel the pull of the gold and decide for itself; a man who has heard of executions at a court decides for himself whether to go there. It also decides how: which arguments to make, what to leave out of a report, what lie to tell, which court to try, what price to ask, and every word it says.
- **Script characters decide by formula** from the same traits, as `ScriptMind` does today. Both kinds are needed anyway, for fallbacks, cheap games and bot-only tables, so the game can watch how and why they diverge: whether a greedy model envoy takes bribes about as often as a greedy script envoy, and when it does not, what reason it gives. That comparison is a result in its own right.
- **Stakes, not dispositions** (decided 20 October 2026, replacing "prime them harder"). If model characters seem too honest, the fix is never to prime them to misbehave. Instead:
  - **Every character wins the same way: wealth.** Gold is his security and his own victory, the ranking of the richest ("Gold is a lifeline"). A model handed a sheet of traits and told to act accordingly meets what look like contradictions (timid, yet hoard gold wherever you can), so the traits are not given to him as a sheet.
  - **His traits become his strategy for winning.** His starting system prompt tells him how a man like him makes his fortune. A loyal, timid man does it through steady, safe paid work and good relations, never risking it all on a gamble; a greedy, bold one through what he can keep from what passes through his hands; a cunning one by selling what he knows; an ambitious one by rising to command, or to a city of his own. One goal and one plan, which a model can follow.
  - **He knows what is at stake:** what a gift's giver expects of him and who would know; the odds of being caught and what follows (dismissal, a name that travels, prison or death); and what honesty earns (the next job at a better fee, the trusted errands, a good name). He gives no gold away, and risks none of his standing, unless he expects it to pay over a time he can name.
  - **Pleasing his host is a stake too.** In the second agent simulation the Haiku envoys' real failing was not honesty but accommodation: 73 commitments made for their lords where the script made 6, and an envoy who promised land beyond his mandate and blamed "my scribe" when the clay did not match. An envoy wants his mission to succeed, which is a motive of a kind; but his fortune rests on his master's trust, and a master who finds his land promised away does not renew him. His request says both: what a successful mission earns him, and what overstepping his mandate costs.
  - **The strategy is where he starts, not a rule.** When his circumstances change (years unpaid, a master who executes envoys, a fortune within reach) he may judge that another way now pays better, so a loyal man can still turn, for reasons. When his traits drift, his strategy is rewritten with them.

  **How the strategy is made** (decided 20 October 2026), in two layers:
  1. **The engine chooses the strategy from the traits, by formula.** A handful of ways to a fortune covers almost everyone: the steady hired man, the man who keeps what passes through his hands, the seller of secrets, the climber who wants command, the man drawn to the outlaw's life. A deterministic rule picks the one, or the two, that best fit a character's traits. It is a fact the engine can test (a timid, loyal man never gets the gambler's way), script characters follow the same strategy in their formulas, so a script and a model character with the same traits pursue the same plan and the comparison of the two minds means something, and it changes only when drifting traits change which strategy fits best.
  2. **A model writes the prompt once, from that strategy and the traits.** It is the narrator's existing task of writing each persona at creation, now telling how this particular man means to get rich, and it reconciles the combinations no template can: a greedy but timid man skims only what nobody will count; a loyal but ambitious one rises by making himself indispensable. One call per character, saved in the game log so replays stay exact, written again only when the strategy changes. It keeps to the traits and the strategy and invents no facts.

  Hand-written templates by trait bands are the fallback when no model is available, as the template narrator is today: ten traits give too many combinations for templates to be anything but generic for most characters and contradictory for the interesting ones.

  **Bold or careful, one goal (decided 21 October 2026).** Every character plays for the same goal, wealth and a high place in the ranking, but not by the same road. Each has an appetite for risk, from his traits, and it becomes part of his strategy:
  - **The bold road:** raids and piracy, high-interest loans to desperate borrowers, well-paid errands into danger. High returns, and a real chance of ending with nothing, or dead.
  - **The careful road:** steady service, loans to strong kings, a hoard kept at a temple. Slower, but it compounds and rarely loses everything.

  Appetite for risk is a way to the goal, never a goal of its own: a bold man takes risks because he judges they pay, not because he likes danger. Both roads must be legitimate. A ranking rewards being high, which favours the bold road's variance; death, which ranks below every living character, punishes it; and the careful road's steady gains keep it in contention. The balance pass (build order item 18) checks this in the script games: bold and careful characters should reach the top of the ranking at comparable rates, and if one road always wins, the numbers are tuned until both pay. Script characters choose their road by formula from their appetite; a model character is told his road in his starting prompt ("How the strategy is made" above) and judges each case for himself.

  In the second agent simulation, the Haiku characters' honesty was partly a correct answer to a world where gold was worth little to them: what gold is good for comes with build order item 11.

**Kings never see skills** (decided 18 October 2026). A king hears what a character says it can do, and checks it the slow way: a background check, a message to a former employer the character names, his own envoys' reports, rumours. Someone a court has dealt with before arrives with data points attached; a stranger arrives with only his own word. The planned employment-history facts give the checks something to find.

- **Lying about identity.** A stranger may claim to be someone he is not, perhaps borrowing a famous negotiator's name and reputation. Every character has a true identity and a claimed one, and each court's records attach to the name it was given. An impostor is exposed when he meets someone who has seen the real man, or when a check turns up the truth, and both take time. The period's own answer is the one Amenhotep III gave Babylon: send someone who knows the person.

**Seeing oneself (decided 21 October 2026).** Skills belong to characters only, and kings see them only through claims and checks ("Kings never see skills"); now the character does not see his own skills as they are either. Each has a hidden self-assessment: some overestimate themselves, some underestimate, most are roughly right. He sees his skills through it, and the engine uses the true ones, as it always does.

- **What he is told is what he believes.** His request gives his skills as he sees them, as beliefs ("you believe you can slip past any guard"), never as facts, and that belief sits in the part of the request that changes, not in the frozen persona, so it can move.
- **The overconfident** take errands beyond them, claim more when they pitch themselves, ask higher fees and are hired more often, and fail more often when it matters; sometimes boldness carries them anyway, since the dice do not care what anyone believes. **The underconfident** undersell themselves, avoid what they could have done and come cheap: hidden gems for a king who tests people rather than believing them.
- **Claims grow ambiguous in a new way.** A character who overstates himself may not be lying; he may believe it. A king cannot tell a liar from a man deceiving himself ("Kings never see skills").
- **In time he may come to doubt it.** His memory records what happened, plainly, as the engine's facts: the missions that failed, the guards who caught him. A model character reads them and may come to question what he believes about himself, or explain them away, as people do. His self-assessment also moves slowly with what happens to him, and the belief in his request moves with it, so script characters learn too. Outcomes follow his true skill on average, so over many errands he drifts towards the truth, but a run of luck misleads him as it misleads everyone else ("A name made of outcomes"). The inclination never quite goes: the overconfident stay a little overconfident, just as a strategy is where a character starts, not a rule ("The strategy is where he starts, not a rule").
- **It is separate from appetite for risk.** A careful man can still think himself brilliant, and a bold one can know exactly what he can do ("Bold or careful, one goal").

For attested people, the sources sometimes give the inclination. Built with the first character package (build order item 10).

**A name made of outcomes (decided 21 October 2026).** What others know of a character is what they saw happen, never his skill and never his luck. The engine records outcomes as facts (an errand done, gold brought home, a guard slipped past, a capture) and they spread as news and rumour like any other ("Information as a structured asset").

- **Luck makes reputations.** A man who never met an enemy army and whose rolls went his way is spoken of as very able; a skilled man with bad luck is spoken of as a failure. Nobody, the man himself included, can see which was skill and which was chance.
- **A name has a price.** Kings hire by reputation, so a famous name asks a higher fee and gets the errands that matter, which is where luck runs out. A king who tests people ("Kings never see skills") can see past a name; one who trusts rumour pays for it.
- **Rumours bend as they travel.** In the spoken word a tale grows with retelling and ages with distance, so a name abroad may be larger, or older, than the man. A character can also spread tales of his own success, or a rival's failures, which is a claim like any other.
- **The man believes it too.** His own record moves his self-assessment ("Seeing oneself"), so the lucky grow overconfident and the unlucky doubt themselves, each with reason.

Built with the first character package (build order item 10), on the news of item 7.

**Declaring a name** (decided 18 October 2026). The engine can only record a lie it can see, so a name works like gold. When a character first meets a court, by pitching or arriving, it declares a name in a structured field. Its own name is the default; giving another character's name or an invented one is a deliberate choice. The engine knows the truth, so it records the false claim, and an exposed impostor gains a fact such as "posed as Hane at Hattusa". A model character chooses for itself, informed by its persona; a script character follows a formula (dishonest, cunning, or carrying a bad name it wants to escape). A claim made in free text ("I am Pharaoh's interpreter") is only talk, like a spoken offer: kings may believe it or not, but a court's records attach only to the declared name. Text never changes state.

**A past before the game, then a past made in play** (decided 18 October 2026). With no history at the start, every character would be bare traits, the first seasons blank and background checks empty. So characters begin with a few seeded ties standing in for the life they lived before, giving asymmetry from day one. Each must have a mechanical hook, never flavour alone:

- **a sympathy for a court** shapes its choices, as today;
- **a debt** puts pressure on its purse and gives the creditor leverage;
- **a lover or family at a court** draws it there and gives that court a hold over it.

Keep them few. After the start, everything new emerges from play and is recorded only when an engine-visible act happens: skimming, defection, detention, a false name declared and exposed, long years abroad. Lies told in free text are not facts; they stay in the message trail for kings to judge. Greedy and dishonest characters therefore accumulate a past, and checks can find it.

**What servants know** (chosen direction, 18 October 2026). Knowledge is a character's capital. The engine records exactly what passed through each person's hands: every tablet a scribe wrote or read, every mandate an envoy carried, every audience he sat through, every tablet he saw sealed. What a servant knows is therefore a fact, not a guess, and it travels with him, in his memory and as a record the engine can draw on. He knows what he saw and nothing more: a scribe knows his king's tablets, not his troop orders, unless the king told him.

- **Trust and danger grow together.** The longer a scribe or envoy serves, the more he knows and the more a rival would pay for him. The most trusted servant is the largest liability.
- **Leaving is a threat.** A dismissed, unpaid or poached servant takes his master's correspondence with him to the next court; "former employees carry secrets" becomes sharp once scribes exist. A fee due on his return is one way to keep him close.
- **Capture is questioning.** A captured envoy or scribe can be questioned. How much the questioning draws out is an engine roll on his courage and loyalty against the effort spent; what he says is his own decision, and he may lie, which is a choice with a motive like any other. A script character tells the truth or lies by formula from his traits.
- **Knowledge is for sale.** A servant who has left, or who is bribed while still serving, can offer what he knows as a structured report (see "Information as an asset"): a true copy of a tablet he wrote, or a convincing forgery of one he never saw. The buyer cannot easily tell which.
- **Kings learn to compartmentalize.** Keep a secret out of the letter and give it to the envoy by mouth; send different servants to different courts; never let one man see both sides of a double game. Each choice trades convenience against exposure, which is real statecraft and needs no rule.
- **Silencing has a price.** Executing a man because he knows too much travels as a rumour, by the same carriers as any other, and a court known for it finds hiring harder, as with executions of liars.

Nothing here needs a new system: it follows from what the engine already records, characters' memory and facts, rumours that need carriers, and characters deciding for themselves. What it needs is the engine's record of who saw what, and questioning as a captive order.

**What skills cover** (decided 18 October 2026). Personality, not skill, decides the urge to alter a message ("Skills are hard-coded; decisions belong to the character"). Skills cover what the engine decides, and few belong to one profession; all shape what a character picks up and escapes on the road:

- gathering information (what an envoy or spy notices, and how accurately);
- avoiding detection and capture;
- spotting forgeries, including assaying gold: an assay is done by one of the court's people, and a poor assayer may miss a good alloy or wrongly accuse honest gold;
- making forgeries, including debasing gold: the king decides whether to cheat and how far, and the worker's skill decides how well the alloy passes inspection (gold changed hands by weight, so cheating meant alloying it with silver or copper; Babylon complained of Egyptian gold that looked like silver);
- commanding armies (the size of a commander's tactical search);
- languages, a skill of 0–100 in each, and an aptitude for learning them (see "Languages").
